name: Everyday Object Histories
description: Fifty ordinary household objects, each with twenty materially distinct chapter angles, for long compilations that tell the true history of a thing slowly. Built for calm, hook-free narration that ends every chapter on a settled image.

exclusions: No invented named individuals and no exact dated events; keep people anonymous and time at the scale of decades and centuries.
No brand names, company names, or trademarks, whether as objects, makers, or mechanisms.
No hooks, cliffhangers, countdowns, or alarm, and nothing that asks the listener to stay awake for what comes next.
No dwelling on suffering, injury, or cruelty; note hard working conditions plainly in a sentence and move on.
Keep every chapter self-contained and resolving to a quiet close, with no callbacks to other chapters and no running arc.
No present-day comparisons that jolt the listener back to the current moment, and no direct address that carries urgency.
prompt_context: Each chapter is the true history of one ordinary object, told slowly to a listener who is drifting toward sleep. Take a single definite period and region for each beat and stay inside it before moving on, so the listener is never asked to hold two places at once. Favour material detail over plot: what the thing was made of, what it weighed in the hand, how the workshop sounded and smelled, what it cost in the money of its time, where it wore thin and how it was mended. Explain a process in the order the work was actually done, and let the pace of the sentences follow the pace of the work. Name the kind of record a surprising detail rests on, briefly, and let it pass; say once and calmly where the record is thin, then continue. Do not open with a question, a promise, or a hook, and do not build tension, because nothing in the chapter needs to be waited for. Never address the listener with urgency and never ask them to remember anything. Close each chapter on a settled image of the object at rest in its own century, so the ending feels like a door pulled quietly to rather than a summary.

idea_axes.label: Object-history lens
values: who was allowed to own one
what it cost and what it was taxed at
how it travelled to the household
what it was called and why the name changed
how it was mended and reused
how it changed the room around it
what replaced it and how slowly
what it left behind in the ground

tuples.episode_object: a two-tined iron sweetmeat fork with a turned bone handle
tuples.time_place_scope: a Byzantine court dining hall in Constantinople across the 1000s
tuples.mechanism: a foreign table habit arriving through a marriage household and meeting clerical suspicion before it settled
tuples.evidence_lens: court chronicles and clerical complaint writing taken as a genre rather than as single reports

tuples.episode_object: a slender silver suckett fork tipped with a small bowl at the far end
tuples.time_place_scope: an English gentry banqueting house at the close of the 1500s
tuples.mechanism: sugar arriving as a costly import and drawing purpose-made tools around it so sweetmeats could be lifted cleanly
tuples.evidence_lens: probate inventories that list plate by weight together with household confectionery accounts

tuples.episode_object: a four-tined steel table fork with a pistol-grip handle of stained horn
tuples.time_place_scope: a Parisian dining room during the change of service styles in the 1800s
tuples.mechanism: courses served one after another instead of all at once, which multiplied the utensils laid at every place
tuples.evidence_lens: printed table-service manuals and cutlery pattern books read as a class of trade literature

tuples.episode_object: a long wooden flesh fork with two blunt prongs for lifting meat from a cauldron
tuples.time_place_scope: an Alpine farmhouse kitchen through the long winters of the 1600s
tuples.mechanism: the fork's older working life as a hearth tool, centuries before it was thought fit for the table
tuples.evidence_lens: excavated kitchen assemblages alongside farm household inventories taken at a tenant's death

tuples.episode_object: an electroplated nickel silver fork stamped with a hotel crest on the stem
tuples.time_place_scope: a British railway hotel dining room in the 1880s

compatibility_rules: Pair only with a compilation formula whose chapters are independent and are ordered by nothing stronger than a shared room, material, or task.
One subject supplies at most one chapter per video; build sibling chapters from different subjects rather than stacking two angles on the same object.
Do not let a chapter transition promise, preview, or refer back to another chapter, because each one has to end before the next begins.
evidence_expectations: Anchor every claim to a named region and a decade or century range, and prefer a phrase such as by the middle of the century over any exact date.
Lean on kinds of records rather than particular titles or authors, and name the kind of record plainly whenever a detail would otherwise sound invented.
Where the record is thin, uneven, or disputed, say so once in a calm sentence and carry on rather than filling the gap with speculation.
Prefer material specifics that survive in objects and accounts, such as weights, materials, prices in period money, and wear patterns, over reconstructed motives.
